entry.title: How Nmap Works: Inside the Source Code of the World’s Most Famous Port Scanner

link.title: How Nmap Works: Inside the Source Code of the World’s Most Famous Port Scanner

entry.content:
You run nmap -sV -sC against a /24 and thirty seconds later the terminal prints open ports, product names, and script findings for hundreds of hosts. Nothing in that output was hardcoded. No engineer sat down and wrote “probe 443 first, then 80.” One function and one loop decided every packet: which port, in what order, at what rate, with how many retries. That function is ultra_scan in scan_engine.cc, and once you have read it, every flag on the Nmap man page turns into a parameter you can explain.

The frustration that drives people into the source is always the same trio of symptoms: a port reports open|filtered on one host and plain filtered on the next; version detection prints http? where a browser sees nginx; a script fires on host A but not on the identical host B. Guessing fixes none of this, because the answers are state transitions inside C++ objects, not configuration knobs. You have to see the objects.

So we cloned nmap/nmap at master — commit 68739db8e4ec, checked out on 2026-11-14 — and followed that one command from argv to report. Every symbol below links to the file and line it occupies today, so you can verify any claim in two clicks. The tour deliberately sticks to the scanning core: targeting, the probe engine, the port state store, version detection, OS fingerprinting, and the script engine.

Nmap's master loop: nmap_main sequences targeting, the probe engine, detection passes, and three NSE script phases around a shared port-state store.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • nmap_main, L1862 parses every option, then runs a master loop that fetches host groups and executes each scan phase against them.
  • -T0..-T5 parsing, L1376 shows that timing templates are just preset assignments: T0 sets scan_delay to 300000 ms at L1381, T4 allows six retransmissions at L1402, T5 cuts that to two at L1412.
  • HostGroupState, L324 batches targets, and get_next_host, L452 yields each group’s hosts while skipping excluded ones.
  • getpts, L129 turns -p expressions into the scan_lists structure the engine consumes.
  • ultra_scan, L2735 is the single scheduler behind SYN, UDP, ACK and every other port scan; nmap_main calls it once per selected type starting at L2236.
  • UltraProbe, L153 is one schedulable probe of type UP_IP, UP_CONNECT, UP_ARP or UP_ND, sent through send_ip_packet, L411.
  • PortList::setPortState, L459 records the open/closed/filtered verdicts, and statenum2str, L941 renders exactly the strings you see in output.
  • After port scans, service_scan, L2790 and OSScan::os_scan, L3519 enrich the results, while open_nse, L940 has already booted the Lua VM for script phases.

The detail view: inside ultra_scan's probe loop, the version-detection queues, the OS fingerprint chain, and the Lua coroutine scheduler that NSE scripts live in.

One loop in nmap.cc decides the order of everything

nmap_main (nmap.cc, L1862) is where coordination lives. Two early lines are the most surprising in the whole file: when you pass -sV, the code sets o.scriptversion = true at L2101, and that flag alone triggers open_nse() at L2104. Version detection and the scripting engine are coupled from the very start — NSE’s Lua VM is booted before the first probe flies, even when you never typed --script.

Then the master loop runs the phases in fixed order per host group: each requested scan type through ultra_scan (L2236 through L2269, covering SYN, ACK, Window, FIN, Xmas, Null, Maimon, UDP, connect, SCTP and protocol scans), then service_scan at L2293, then OS detection at L2298, then the main script pass at L2307 and a post-scan pass at L2368. The pre-scan script phase ran even earlier, at L2110. Scripts therefore execute three separate times against the same target set — prerule, hostrule/portrule, postrule. Idle and FTP-bounce scans are the exceptions; the comment at L2271 admits they “can only handle one target at a time.”

ultra_scan is one scheduler, not thirteen

Every port scan type funnels into one function: void ultra_scan(std::vector<Target *> &Targets, const struct scan_lists *ports, stype scantype, struct timeout_info *to) at scan_engine.cc, L2735. It builds an UltraScanInfo at L2753 holding all per-host and global state, then calls begin_sniffer at L2780 only for raw scans. That conditional is why -sT (connect scan) works without root privileges: no pcap needed, replies arrive on real sockets.

The heartbeat is the loop at L2784: doAnyPings, doAnyOutstandingRetransmits, doAnyRetryStackRetransmits, then doAnyNewProbes (L2789–L2794). The order is deliberate — the source comments that retry-stack retransmits run after outstanding ones “for memory consumption reasons.” Retransmission is capped per probe: the check at L701 only allows another resend while probe->get_tryno() < maxval.

Pacing is not a sleep loop. ultra_timing_vals::ack and drop (timing.cc, L221, L244) rescale the send rate on every response or timeout, using thresholds from scan_performance_vars::init at L267. The -T presets just seed this machinery: T0 means one probe at a time with a five-minute scan_delay (L1381); T4 sets an RTT window of 100–1250 ms and caps the TCP scan delay at 10 ms (L1396–L1399); T5 allows a fifteen-minute host timeout but only two retransmissions (L1408, L1412). Notably, UDP is deliberately excluded from scan-delay caps in both T4 and T5 — the comments at L1401 and L1411 cite ICMP rate limiting and unreliability.

The port state machine is six strings and one function

Everything Nmap prints about a port resolves through statenum2str (portlist.cc, L941): open, filtered, unfiltered, closed, open|filtered, closed|filtered, otherwise unknown. That is the entire user-visible vocabulary. PortList::setPortState (L459) records transitions and hands back the old state, which is how the engine knows whether a port flipped mid-scan.

open|filtered deserves the repeatable insight: it exists for probe types where silence is ambiguous. A TCP SYN to a closed port gets a RST back (closed); silence means either a firewall dropped it or the service never answers UDP — so UDP and protocol scans leave ports in the combined state. Service detection then writes over the record through PortList::setServiceProbeResults (L307), storing name, version and tunnel info, while addScriptResult (L377) hangs script output off the same port object. One store, three writers, exactly the strings you read on screen.

Version detection: 188 probes and three queues

service_scan (service_scan.cc, L2790) organizes work in a ServiceGroup (L207) with exactly three queues — services_finished, services_in_progress, services_remaining (L211–L213). Each open port gets a ServiceNFO (L111) tracking its pending probe list and collected responses. startNextProbe (L2104) fires from nsock callbacks, sending the next probe only when round-trip timing allows.

The probe menu comes from nmap-service-probes, a single 17,166-line database file containing 188 Probe definitions with the regex match lines that classify banners. When a match hits, results are stored back through setServiceProbeResults at L2734 and L2774. Because -sV also switched on scriptversion, NSE service scripts contribute their findings into the same record.

How NSE threads attach to the scan

open_nse (nse_main.cc, L940) enforces hard engineering constraints: it refuses to run on anything below Lua 5.4 (L956), caps total Lua allocations at 400 MB via AllocState(400 * 1024 * 1024) (L964), and installs a five-second per-thread interrupt timer (L967) so a runaway script cannot freeze the scan. Entry into script land is script_scan (L992), which pushes run_main (L1000) and calls it through lua_pcall with the targets vector passed as light userdata.

On the Lua side, main(hosts, scantype) (nse_main.lua, L1451) drives everything. get_chosen_scripts (L730) resolves -sC and --script specs against script.db. The threads_iters table (L1393) spawns one coroutine per matching rule: prerule threads for pre-scan, hostrule and portrule threads per host and per port at L1409 and L1418, postrule threads last. The portrule loop iterates cnse.ports(host) at L1416 — the very ports the state machine classified. The scheduler run(threads_iter) (L905) resumes coroutines as their sockets become ready. So -sC is not magic: it is a coroutine pool reading the same PortList your output is rendered from.

From configure.ac to a single binary

The top-level build is classic autotools: configure.ac plus aclocal.m4, config.guess, and Makefile.in generate the makefile, with RPM specs (nmap.spec.in, zenmap.spec.in) and a BSDmakefile alongside. The CMakeLists.txt files that exist in the tree live only inside the vendored dependency folders — libpcap, libpcre, libz, libssh2, libdnet-stripped — not at the root. Those dependencies default to vendored copies: configure.ac offers --with-libpcap=included and friends, documented as “Always use the version included with Nmap.” The Lua runtime itself is carried in-tree via nse_lua.h, with lpeg.c at the root for pattern matching.

Two build quirks we observed while touring. First, the repository is a 2,611-file monorepo: it carries ncat/, zenmap/, and 619 .nse scripts under scripts/ next to the scanner core. Second, the -T option parser opens with a deliberately obfuscated one-liner at nmap.cc, L1377 — pointer arithmetic that mangles the argument in place — before falling into the readable if/else chain quoted above. All line numbers in this post were verified against master at 68739db8e4ec on 2026-11-14.

If this way of reading systems appeals to you, three more pyshine tours pair naturally with it: Redis runs a similarly single-threaded event loop over a completely different data model; NATS shows what fan-out and flow control look like when the scheduler lives in the protocol; and Traefik is worth the opposite comparison — routing instead of probing, with the same obsession over who gets sent what, when.

Honest Limits

  • Every symbol and line number was verified against master at commit 68739db8e4ec (cloned 2026-11-14). They will drift as the project moves; re-derive from the current tree before quoting them in patches.
  • The tour covers the scanning core only. ncat/, zenmap/, and the 619 NSE scripts under scripts/ are substantial subsystems we did not read here.
  • No benchmark numbers appear because none were measured: every timing figure cited (300000 ms delay, 400 MB cap, five-second script timer) is a source constant, not a performance result.
  • The “one scheduler” claim covers the mainstream raw and connect scans. Idle scan and FTP bounce scan are separate single-target paths, flagged as such in the source at L2271.
  • The -sV → NSE coupling (L2101–L2104) means the clean phase diagram hides one edge: scriptversion scripts run during version detection. We flag it; we did not trace that sub-path line by line.
entry.summary: How Nmap works, traced through its real C++ source: the ultra_scan scheduler, port state machine, -T timing presets, version detection and NSE hooks.

entry.title: How Audacity Saves a Two-Hour Project in Seconds: the Block-File Store and the Real-Time Playback Engine

link.title: How Audacity Saves a Two-Hour Project in Seconds: the Block-File Store and the Real-Time Playback Engine

entry.content:
Record a two-hour multitrack session, let the machine crash, reopen the project, and press Ctrl+S with a hundred undo levels stacked up. Editors that treat a project as one big file must rewrite megabytes of waveform data to persist a few seconds of new recording. Audacity does not, and the difference is not an incremental-save heuristic bolted onto the file format — it is the file format. Since Audacity 3.0, a .aup3 project is a single SQLite database, and the audio itself lives in rows the code explicitly treats as immutable: written once, never updated, only ever deleted.

That design turns saving into a metadata operation. Waveform blocks are committed to the database from the moment recording touched them, so a save only replaces one small row holding a binary-XML snapshot of the project structure. The same immutability makes undo cheap — an undo step is a pointer shuffle over existing blocks — and the schema keeps a rolling archive of past documents for crash recovery.

The second half happens in real time, dozens of times per second. One worker thread pulls decoded blocks out of SQLite, resamples them, runs realtime effects, and pushes the result into ring buffers, while the PortAudio callback thread drains those buffers straight to your sound card under hard latency deadlines. If you have written capture software you know this discipline — our OBS Studio tour covers the same never-block-the-callback rules for video. This post reads the actual Audacity source on master and follows both halves: the block store and the playback engine.

Overview: the Audacity 4 QML shell delegates into the legacy au3 core, where transport, track model and the SQLite block store meet the real-time audio engine.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • The new Qt/QML interface in src/projectscene drives intents through a thin wrapper — au3project.cpp hosts a complete legacy AudacityProject inside the new application.
  • Clicking Play lands in ProjectAudioManager::PlayCurrentRegion, L472, which assembles a bundle of playback sequences and hands it to the audio engine.
  • The engine opens the device with Pa_OpenStream, L689 and registers audacityAudioCallback, L2725 as the entry point PortAudio will call on every buffer.
  • Sample production happens on a dedicated worker through Mixer::Process, L292, which resamples and format-converts each slice before it enters the ring buffers.
  • Realtime effect processing is applied per track through RealtimeEffectManager::Process, L122, whose states run on the same producer thread.
  • Reads sink into WaveTrack::DoGet, L2958, which walks the track’s clips to satisfy a request for samples.
  • Each clip delegates to Sequence::FindBlock, L1026, a smart-search over the block array that locates the single block holding any requested sample.
  • The blocks themselves are rows described by ProjectFileSchema, L114 — four tables including sampleblocks — and written by SqliteSampleBlock::Commit, L743.

Detail: the producer thread (slices, mixer, effects) and the callback thread (fill output, meters) meet at the ring buffers, while every sample ultimately traces back to an immutable SQLite row.

A project file that is really a SQLite database

Open a .aup3 file in any SQLite browser and you will find the schema baked into the source at ProjectFileSchema, L114. There are four tables. The project table holds one row — id is always 1 — containing a dictionary blob and a binary-XML document blob, with field names replaced by two-byte dictionary indices for speed. The autosave table has the same shape and holds crash-recovery snapshots. The sampleblocks table is where audio lives: blockid, sampleformat, three summary columns (summin, summax, sumrms), two precomputed min/max/RMS overview blobs (summary256, summary64k) and the samples BLOB itself. Finally, project_history keeps the last ten saved documents — the depth is the constant at kProjectHistoryDepth, L112 — so a corrupt document can be rolled back to an earlier good one.

The decisive comment sits right above the table definition: “Rows are immutable – never updated after addition, but may be deleted” (ProjectFileIO.cpp, L171). Because rows never change, the database can run in WAL mode with wal_autocheckpoint disabled — see the pragma block at DBConnection.cpp, L33, which also sets synchronous = NORMAL and a five-second busy timeout — and when the project closes, a final checkpoint, L280 runs sqlite3_wal_checkpoint_v2 with SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_TRUNCATE to fold the write-ahead log into the main file.

Saving follows from the design. ProjectFileIO::UpdateSaved, L2288 serializes the project to binary XML and calls WriteDoc("project", doc) — replacing one row, not rewriting waveforms. First-time saves are handled by ProjectFileIO::SaveProject, L2311, which fast-paths promoting a temporary project by renaming the file. The one operation that does copy data is compaction: deleted blocks leave free pages behind, so ShouldCompact, L1281 decides when bloat justifies a copy through Compact at ProjectFileIO.cpp, L1602. Readers of our HandBrake tour will recognize the pattern: keep the expensive payload append-only and treat structure changes as cheap metadata.

Blocks, not byte streams: how Sequence chops your audio

The unit of storage is not the track or the clip but the block. A WaveClip owns one Sequence per channel — visible in the constructor at WaveClip.cpp, L231, where mSequences.resize(width) allocates a sequence for every channel of a stereo clip. A Sequence is an array of SeqBlock entries, each pointing at one sample block and its start offset.

Block sizing derives from one static: Sequence::sMaxDiskBlockSize, L46 defaults to 1048576 bytes (1 MiB, adjustable via SetMaxDiskBlockSize), and the constructor computes mMinSamples = sMaxDiskBlockSize / SAMPLE_SIZE(...) / 2 and mMaxSamples = mMinSamples * 2 at Sequence.cpp, L55. For 32-bit float audio that is between 131,072 and 262,144 samples per block — roughly three to six seconds at 44.1 kHz. Incoming runs are consolidated into properly sized blocks by Sequence::Blockify, L1534, and every mutation ends in AppendBlocksIfConsistent, L1812, which validates the array before it becomes visible.

Locating a sample is deliberately clever. Sequence::FindBlock, L1026 is not a plain binary search; the inline comment explains it is a “dictionary search” that guesses the target block proportionally to sample position, because blocks created later tend to hold later samples. Once found, Sequence::Read, L1076 calls GetSamples on the block, and the zero-copy variant GetFloatSampleView, L1096 hands back views of whole blocks instead of copying them.

On the storage side, SqliteSampleBlockFactory, L134 creates and deduplicates blocks, while SqliteSampleBlock::Commit, L743 binds the samples, format and the two summary blobs into the INSERT for the sampleblocks table. Reading back goes through SqliteSampleBlock::Load, L680, a SELECT by blockid. This is also the recording path: during capture, the audio layer calls sequence->Append at AudioIO.cpp, L2662, which flows into WaveTrack::Append, L2564 — so recorded audio is committed block by block as you speak, not held in memory until you stop.

One lap around the audio callback

Playback runs on two threads that meet at ring buffers. The worker is a plain std::thread started at AudioIO.cpp, L307 running AudioIO::AudioThread, L1908, which loops whenever playback buffers run low. Its work starts at FillPlayBuffers, L2005 and funnels into ProcessPlaybackSlices, L2097. Each iteration asks the scheduling policy for a slice via PlaybackPolicy::GetPlaybackSlice, L90, then calls mixer->Process at AudioIO.cpp, L2143. Inside the mixer, MixerSource::MixVariableRates, L68 pulls raw samples with GetFloats at MixerSource.cpp, L132, multiplies them by the track envelope, and resamples to the device rate. The comment in ProcessPlaybackSlices is refreshingly honest: this mixer “isn’t actually mixing” — it does resampling, format conversion and time-track warping; true summing happens later.

Meanwhile, the PortAudio callback thread runs audacityAudioCallback, L2725, delegating to AudioIoCallback::AudioCallback, L3344. That function polls mute/solo state, feeds the input meter while recording, and hands off to FillOutputBuffers, L2783, which drains the ring buffers into PortAudio’s float output, applies the software volume and copies meter data, clamping everything to [-1.0, +1.0]. The time-queue update at AudioIO.cpp, L2129 is explicitly ordered before the sample writes so the UI’s play-head never reads ahead of the audio. For the same callback discipline in a minimal C++ media stack, our SFML tour is a good companion read.

Where realtime effects live in the processing chain

Effects that must respond while audio plays — the ones whose sliders you drag during playback — are managed per track by RealtimeEffectManager. When a stream starts, RealtimeEffectManager::Initialize, L53 instantiates every state at the stream’s sample rate and buffer size. The UI adds and removes effects through AddState, L241 without stopping playback, because each RealtimeEffectState is an independently swappable slot. Processing happens on the producer thread, not inside the PortAudio callback: ProcessPlaybackSlices calls the processing scope at AudioIO.cpp, L2229 after all slices have been staged, and RealtimeEffectManager::Process, L122 walks the states with state.Process(...) at RealtimeEffectManager.cpp, L154. The DSP work itself is done by effect implementations derived from EffectBase.cpp, whose per-block overrides execute inside this audio worker — an effect author’s code runs with the same real-time constraints as the mixer.

From a wxWidgets-era 3.x codebase to a Qt 6.11 master

A few facts worth knowing before you clone the repository. master is now Audacity 4.0 development — version.cmake declares 4.0.0 with MUSE_APP_UNSTABLE ON and the identifier org.audacityteam.audacity4, and the changelog calls Audacity 4 “a ground-up rebuild on the Qt framework”. Everything toured above still lives in the tree, but relocated: the 3.x-era core sits under au3/ with libraries renamed to an au3-* convention (au3-wave-track, au3-audio-io, au3-project-file-io), while the new QML application occupies src/. The build stack per BUILDING.md is CMake with Ninja as the tested generator, Qt 6.11 (the Windows build expects the “MSVC 2022 64-bit” flavor) and macOS 13+ with Xcode 15+. Two Git submodules — muse and muse_deps, pointing into the MuseScore muse_framework — supply the framework the new shell builds on, which is why BUILDING.md leans on MuseScore’s setup guide. On Windows, generate_sln.bat produces a Visual Studio solution if you prefer that over driving CMake yourself. One branch quirk from the README: master is in “major structural change”, so patches to the 3.x series must branch off audacity3 instead.

Honest Limits

Everything cited above is pinned to master on the day of writing, and the README warns that the branch is undergoing major structural change — line numbers will drift as the AU4 refactor continues, and the glue in src/au3wrap is among the most actively edited areas. This tour covers the au3 audio core in depth and the new QML shell only at its delegation boundary. The “two-hour project saves in seconds” framing is an architectural consequence of immutable rows plus the doc-only rewrite in UpdateSaved, not a benchmark we ran — disk speed, block count and the compaction threshold (ShouldCompact) modulate real numbers. Block-size arithmetic derives from the 1 MiB default of sMaxDiskBlockSize, a settable static rather than a guarantee. And realtime effect processing in this build runs on the buffer-exchange worker thread, not the PortAudio callback thread itself — trust ProcessPlaybackSlices over older write-ups.
entry.summary: A source tour of audacity/audacity on GitHub: how the .aup3 SQLite block store makes saves nearly free, and what happens inside the audio thread on every playback callback.

entry.title: Inside FFmpeg: A Source Tour of the Demux, Decode, Filter, Encode and Mux Threads

link.title: Inside FFmpeg: A Source Tour of the Demux, Decode, Filter, Encode and Mux Threads

entry.content:
Run ffmpeg -i fourk.mov -c:v libx264 -crf 23 out.mp4 on a long 4K clip and the machine hums for an hour. The only visible feedback is that one line ticking upward: frame= 48211 fps= 41 q=23.0 size= .... It looks like a single loop. It is not. Inside the process, compressed packets, raw frames and encoded packets are being pushed through several queues between threads that start, block and finish independently of each other.

The interesting part is what happens to one single frame. It gets read off disk as a compressed packet, handed to a decoder thread, pulled out as raw pixels, pushed into a filter graph — your -vf scale=1920:1080 lives there — dragged back out, fed into the encoder, and finally interleaved into the output container by yet another thread. None of these stages sit in a straight line inside one function; they coordinate through a scheduler in fftools/ffmpeg_sched.c.

This tour follows that flow through the current master sources, and every claim links to a specific line on GitHub so you can click through and argue with it. If you enjoy watching real codebases from the inside, our earlier looks at the SDL window-and-events core, the LÖVE2D Lua runtime, and Godot engine internals make good companion reading.

The whole transcode flow on master: main() and transcode() orchestrate, the scheduler gives every stage its own thread, and data moves demux → decode → filter → encode → mux through scheduler queues. Each node maps to a real file in the repository.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • main() is a dispatcher, not a worker. main, L995 allocates the scheduler, parses options and hands off to transcode() — the whole file is only about 1,070 lines long.
  • transcode() owns the main loop. transcode, L901 starts every worker with sch_start(), then loops on sch_wait(), printing the famous frame= fps= q= line via print_report().
  • The scheduler turns each stage into a thread. task_start, L414 calls pthread_create() once per demuxer, decoder, filter graph, encoder and muxer task.
  • The demuxer thread reads the input. input_thread, L843 loops on av_read_frame() and routes each packet through demux_send(), applying bitstream filters on the way.
  • libavformat does the container parsing. av_read_frame, L1646 funnels down to ff_read_packet(), where MOV, MKV and TS plug in their own per-container callbacks.
  • Decoding is push-then-pull. decoder_thread, L909 blocks on sch_dec_receive() for the next packet, then packet_decode() calls avcodec_send_packet() and pulls decoded frames back out.
  • The filter graph runs in its own thread. filter_thread, L3507 receives frames, lazily builds and configures the graph, feeds it via buffersrc and drains buffersink toward the encoder.
  • The muxer thread interleaves and writes. muxer_thread, L401 keeps streams in sync through a SyncQueue and writes through av_interleaved_write_frame().

The detail view: 34 functions across seven groups, following one frame from ff_read_packet() all the way to av_interleaved_write_frame(), including every queue crossing between threads.

One process, several threads

The scheduler is the spine. sch_alloc() (ffmpeg_sched.c, L625) sets up a table of task nodes; the node kinds are enumerated in fftools/ffmpeg_sched.h as SCH_NODE_TYPE_DEMUX through SCH_NODE_TYPE_FILTER_OUT (L93). sch_start() (L1767) walks the table and calls task_start() on each node — that is where pthread_create() happens (L425). From this point the main thread stops doing media work: transcode() just waits on sch_wait() (L1833), handles keyboard interaction and prints periodic reports.

What crosses between threads? Packets and frames, through queues owned by the scheduler: sch_dec_send() (L2419) publishes decoded frames to whichever filter graph consumes them, sch_filter_receive() (L2581) is the blocking pull on the filter side, sch_filter_send() (L2659) hands filtered frames to the encoder, and sch_enc_send() (L2532) routes compressed packets toward the muxer. Registration happens long before any thread starts: ifile_open() (ffmpeg_demux.c, L2318) calls sch_add_demux() with input_thread as the function pointer. Bitstream filters run on the demuxer side too, before a packet is queued: demux_send() pushes each one through the bsf chain built by do_bsf_graph() (L615), so something like an annex-B conversion never blocks a decode thread. That design explains what you see in htop during a transcode: no thread does everything, and each one spends much of its life blocked on a queue.

The queues themselves are shallow on purpose. queue_alloc() (L382) builds them on top of fftools/thread_queue.c, and the default depths are tiny: DEFAULT_PACKET_THREAD_QUEUE_SIZE is 2 (ffmpeg_sched.h, L257) and DEFAULT_FRAME_THREAD_QUEUE_SIZE is 2 (L262). A slow filter thread therefore applies backpressure all the way to the demuxer instead of letting the process balloon in memory — one reason ffmpeg transcodes hour-long files without eating your RAM.

Packet in, frame out: the decode loop

decoder_thread() (ffmpeg_dec.c, L909) is a tight loop: block on sch_dec_receive() (L924), then call packet_decode() (L950). packet_decode() pushes the packet in with avcodec_send_packet() (L719) and loops on avcodec_receive_frame_flags() (L749) until the codec has nothing more to give. Inside libavcodec, avcodec_send_packet() (decode.c, L738) buffers the packet and decode_receive_frame_internal() (L669) drives decode_simple_receive_frame() (L617) until a frame pops out.

One drift worth knowing: on current master, avcodec_receive_frame() itself no longer lives in decode.c — it is defined in libavcodec/avcodec.c, L718. If your local tree is older, look in decode.c; if newer, look in avcodec.c. Decoded frames leave through sch_dec_send() (called at L820), which wakes the filtergraph thread. That is the entire decode stage: packets in, frames out, one dedicated thread per decoder.

The filtergraph thread

filter_thread() (L3507) does three jobs. First it lazily builds the graph: the first frame triggers configure_filtergraph() (called at L3523, defined at L2187), which allocates an AVFilterGraph, inserts a buffersrc per graph input and a buffersink per output (L1751 for video, L1882 for audio), then calls avfilter_graph_config() (L2268) to negotiate pixel and sample formats. Second it feeds frames: send_frame() (L3242, called from the loop at L3575) pushes into buffersrc. Third it drains: read_frames() pulls results via av_buffersink_get_frame_flags() (L2934) and hands each one to sch_filter_send() (L2891).

Underneath, libavfilter does the real work. avfilter_graph_config() (avfiltergraph.c, L1480) runs the negotiation; after that, each push into buffersrc triggers ff_filter_graph_run_once() (L1675, reached from buffersrc.c, L212), which advances one activation — and filter_frame_to_filter() (avfilter.c, L1202) is where your filter’s code finally executes. Every -vf option you have ever typed is processed here, one frame at a time.

Encode, sync, mux

The encoder mirrors the decoder. encoder_thread() (ffmpeg_enc.c, L998) blocks on sch_enc_receive() (L1026) for the next frame, and frame_encode() (L867) drives encode_frame() (L683), which calls avcodec_send_frame() (L722) and loops on avcodec_receive_packet() (L734). Encoded packets leave via sch_enc_send() (L529) toward the muxer thread. Subtitle encoders open immediately (L1019); audio and video encoders open lazily on their first frame through enc_open() (L413), triggered by a scheduler callback.

The muxer thread (muxer_thread(), L401) pulls packets with sch_mux_receive() (L420) and keeps streams interleaved through sync_queue_process() (L244): sq_send() at L249, sq_receive() at L258 — the SyncQueue API itself lives in fftools/sync_queue.c (L343, L596). Writing goes through write_packet() → av_interleaved_write_frame() (L230); libavformat’s own av_interleaved_write_frame, L1268 reorders packets by DTS. The container header is written by avformat_write_header, L512 once every stream is ready, and of_write_trailer() (L785) closes things out after sch_stop(). If you pass -c copy, most of this tour is skipped: of_streamcopy() (L454) routes packets demux → mux directly.

From configure script to ffmpeg.exe

Some real build facts from the master tree, observed while preparing this tour:

  • The build starts with configure, an 8,883-line shell script that probes your toolchain, libraries and CPU features before generating config.mak.
  • Hand-written x86 assembly defaults to nasm (x86asmexe_default="nasm", configure, L4415). If it is missing, the script dies with “nasm not found or too old. Please install/update nasm or use –disable-x86asm” (L6757) — and that flag quietly removes most SIMD speedups, which is why nobody ships it in release builds.
  • The binary is assembled from the split modules: fftools/Makefile lists ffmpeg_dec.o, ffmpeg_demux.o, ffmpeg_enc.o, ffmpeg_filter.o, ffmpeg_hw.o, ffmpeg_mux.o, ffmpeg_mux_init.o, ffmpeg_opt.o, ffmpeg_sched.o, sync_queue.o and thread_queue.o as objects for the ffmpeg target. The thread split you saw in the diagrams is visible right in the build file.
  • ffplay builds beside it and is the reason SDL shows up in the dependency graph: configure line 4369 sets ffplay_deps="avcodec avformat avfilter swscale swresample sdl2", and ffplay.c includes SDL_thread.h. ffprobe brings its own textformat/ output modules (tf_json, tf_xml, tf_compact and friends) for machine-readable output.
  • Quirk of the tree itself: the default branch is master, HEAD was a948f8e34a21 at the time of writing, and the repository holds roughly 11,200 tracked files, with the six media libraries and fftools/ living as siblings at the top level.

Honest Limits

  • Every line number here was verified against master at commit a948f8e34a21 (checked 2026-11-13). FFmpeg moves fast, so expect drift — two moves are already visible on this branch: avcodec_receive_frame() now lives in libavcodec/avcodec.c, and avfilter_graph_config() is in libavfilter/avfiltergraph.c, not avfilter.c.
  • This tour covers the generic software path. Hardware acceleration (fftools/ffmpeg_hw.c), the per-container callbacks behind demux.c and mux.c, and the sub-second audio/video sync logic inside the SyncQueue are described only at the level this article needs.
  • No performance numbers are claimed anywhere on purpose: real fps depends on codec, filters, resolution and CPU. The sources show mechanics, not benchmarks.
  • -c copy bypasses most of the story via of_streamcopy() — demux straight to mux, no decode, no filter, no encode.
  • ffplay’s playback loop (window, audio clock sync) is a separate program sharing these libraries and is not covered here; it builds on SDL2 (configure line 4369), which we toured separately.

If you want to trace further on your own, ffprobe.c is the best API tutorial in the repository — a clean, standalone consumer of the same libraries. And the next time a 4K transcode hogs your CPU for an hour, you will know exactly which threads are to blame and where each one blocks.
entry.summary: What ffmpeg actually does frame by frame under a 4K transcode load: a line-linked tour through ffmpeg.c, the scheduler, libavformat, libavcodec and libavfilter on current master.

entry.title: Inside GStreamer: A Source Tour of Elements, Pads and the Caps Bargain

link.title: Inside GStreamer: A Source Tour of Elements, Pads and the Caps Bargain

entry.content:
You wire up a test graph in gst-launch-1.0 — v4l2src ! videoconvert ! x264enc ! mp4mux ! filesink — and it dies with a terse could-not-link complaint between two elements you were sure spoke the same format. You set GST_DEBUG=3, rerun, and the terminal scrolls fifteen thousand lines in two seconds: buffers allocated, pads activated, caps proposed, rejected, re-proposed, elements flipping states one after another. Nothing in that wall of text tells you who decided the topology, or at which exact line a format disagreement became fatal.

The answer, it turns out, is embarrassingly small. Every media operation in GStreamer is an element: a factory-produced object with input and output ports called pads. Elements are parented into bins, the outermost bin owns the clock and hands out base time, and a topologically sorted state walk brings the whole thing alive. Once playing, nothing supervises the data at all — a source thread pushes buffers into a pad, the pad dereferences a function pointer into its peer, and the chain continues element by element until a sink swallows the buffer. If two pads cannot agree on a format, the disagreement is settled by set arithmetic on caps before a single frame flows.

This tour walks that entire journey in the current monorepo on main (pinned at commit 3e358d0e706c), with every claim anchored to a file and line you can click. Two diagrams anchor the story: a compact overview of the machinery, and a detail graph that includes the pad engine, the caps negotiation round and the core test elements.

GStreamer overview, left to right: elements are built by a registry factory, parented into the top-level bin, brought up by a sorted state walk, and then buffers race from the source loop through pad pushes and a caps filter down to a sink — with the bus reporting everything app-ward. Every node links to the real source.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • gst_element_factory_make, L820 — the registry lookup that turns a name like fakesrc into a live element instance.
  • gst_bin_add, L1511 — elements only become part of a processing graph when a bin parents them.
  • Top-level bin ctor, L348 — the outermost bin, the one that selects the clock and distributes base time to everyone beneath it.
  • gst_pad_link_full, L2584 — wiring a source pad to a sink pad, under the link checks the caller requested.
  • gst_element_set_state, L2975 — one call that kicks off the entire READY → PAUSED → PLAYING ascent.
  • bin change_state func, L2819 — the bin relays the transition to its children in topologically sorted order, so sinks change state before sources.
  • gst_base_src_loop, L2885 — the source-side thread that fills buffers and starts the race.
  • gst_pad_push, L5040 — the exact moment a buffer leaves one element for its peer.
  • gst_bus_post, L330 — how every one of these milestones reaches the application.

The detail graph: the pad machinery that moves buffers, the caps negotiation round that guards links, the bin/bus layer that supervises, and the core elements (fakesrc, identity, capsfilter, queue, typefind, fakesink) that make test graphs run.

The element graph: who decides the topology

When you type a !-chain on the command line, the DSL is lexed by parse.l and the generated grammar calls gst_element_factory_make, L820 once per named element. Nothing is wired yet. gst_bin_add, L1511 parents each element into the top-level bin — Top-level bin ctor, L348 — which is just a bin that additionally owns clock selection and base-time bookkeeping. The topology is therefore decided by the caller: the core never infers what you meant to connect.

Bringing it alive is a two-level relay. gst_element_set_state, L2975 on the top-level bin hits the bin implementation at bin change_state func, L2819, which iterates children through gst_bin_iterate_sorted, L2431 — a topological sort so that a sink goes to PAUSED before the source feeding it. Leaf elements commit their transitions one intermediate state at a time via gst_element_continue_state, L2789, which is why an async decoder can take visible time between PAUSED and PLAYING. As each element changes state, its pads are switched on by gst_pad_activate_mode, L1361, which decides per-pad whether data will arrive by pushing (the common case) or by pulling with gst_pad_get_range, L5298.

Buffers in flight: the push path

Once PLAYING, the source thread in gst_base_src_loop, L2885 asks for one buffer of a given length through gst_base_src_get_range, L2563; a concrete source implements the create vmethod — in the core’s own test element that is gst_fake_src_create, L797, which mints empty buffers. The loop then calls gst_pad_push, L5040, which funnels into gst_pad_push_data, L4872: probe callbacks installed by gst_pad_add_probe, L1485 get their chance to inspect, delay or drop the buffer, and only then does gst_pad_chain_data_unchecked, L4574 invoke the function pointer the peer element installed on its sink pad. That is the whole transport layer: a linked list of function-pointer calls across pads, with a GstFlowReturn value flowing back upstream as the only control channel.

Two detours are worth knowing. First, a queue is where one thread ends and another begins: gst_queue_chain, L1435 parks the buffer and wakes a second thread whose gst_queue_loop, L1595 dequeues and pushes onward. Second, pass-through elements like identity do not even own a chain function — gst_identity_transform_ip, L736 mutates the buffer in place inside the base-class machinery, the same pattern FFmpeg’s filtergraph uses for in-place filters (we traced those threads in our FFmpeg tour). At the end of the line, gst_fake_sink_render, L447 consumes and frees.

Caps negotiation: resolving a format mismatch

This is where your could-not-link failure actually happened. Every pad can answer “what formats can you accept?” — gst_pad_query_caps_default, L3345 intersects the pad template’s static caps with whatever filter was set on the pad. During linking, checks compare the two sides with gst_caps_can_intersect, L1945, a cheap existential test: if no structure overlaps, there is no point negotiating. The real merge is gst_caps_intersect_zig_zag, L2021, which walks two caps’ structures in zig-zag order to find the common ground, and gst_caps_is_subset, L1728 is the test that declares a link “fixed” — nothing left to negotiate.

Filters bend the bargain rather than break it. A transform element answers “given the peer wants X, what can I turn it into?” through default transform_caps, L442; capsfilter is the purest form, with gst_capsfilter_transform_caps, L279 simply advertising intersection with the user’s filter. When every element is PAUSED, the state walk described above asks each pad for its final caps, and a link whose intersection collapses to nothing fails — that error is what your terminal was showing. Even mid-flight, an element that receives a buffer outside its agreed caps returns a not-negotiated flow return, and the message surfaces on the bus.

Messages and traces: the bus and GST_DEBUG

The data path is deliberately quiet; reporting happens out of band. Elements emit messages through gst_bus_post, L330 — errors, end-of-stream, state changes, latency questions. Bins intercept child messages in bin handle_message func, L3682, aggregate or act on them (a latency answer triggers gst_bin_recalculate_latency, L2718), and forward the rest. The application side blocks in gst_bus_poll, L1218 or drains with gst_bus_pop, L695 — one shared bus per top-level bin, exactly the edge the overview diagram draws app-ward.

The debug wall you saw is separate machinery in gst_debug_log, L719: category, level, timestamp, object name and the source location of every call. GST_DEBUG=3 simply raises the threshold; the per-buffer chatter you noticed (push/chain lines for every single buffer) comes from the pad functions themselves, and the log can even resolve function pointers to names through _gst_debug_nameof_funcptr, L2841 — which is why the trace shows real symbol names like gst_fake_sink_render instead of hex addresses.

From tarball to topology: build facts

The layout surprised us. Since the monorepo consolidation, the “core” is not at the repository root at all: gstpad.c, gstbin.c and friends live under subprojects/gstreamer/gst/, base classes under subprojects/gstreamer/libs/gst/base/, and the plugin trees for good, bad, ugly and base sit under subprojects/gst-plugins-*/ (confirmed with git ls-tree -r, 13,998 entries). Third-party dependencies arrive as .wrap files — glib.wrap, FFmpeg.wrap, dav1d.wrap, abseil-cpp.wrap — fetched by meson at configure time, alongside gst-plugins-rs.wrap, the plugin set written in Rust (we covered that language’s ecosystem in the Rust tour). subprojects/gstreamer/meson.build declares the version as 1.29.2.1, a development snapshot.

A few quirks worth recording: the gst-launch grammar is generated — gst/parse/parse.l and grammar.y.in are templates fed to gen_grammar.py.in/gen_lex.py.in, so flex/bison run during the build. The typefind element now lives in core (plugins/elements/gsttypefindelement.c) while only the sniffing heuristics remain in base. Size-wise, gstpad.c is the heavyweight at 6,080 lines, versus gstbin.c at 3,934, gstelement.c at 3,371, gstcaps.c at 2,844 and gstbus.c at just 1,273 — the dataflow engine dwarfs everything, which the detail diagram reflects. One practical note: a sparse clone must use the subprojects/... paths; a naive sparse-checkout of a top-level gst/ materializes almost nothing, which is exactly how we discovered the reorganization.

Honest Limits

  • Every line number is pinned to main at commit 3e358d0e706c (checked 2026-11-13); gstpad.c is actively developed and these anchors will drift.
  • We traced push-mode flow end to end; pull mode exists (activation chooses it, get_range serves it) but its task and scheduling plumbing is not drawn in either diagram.
  • The diagrams cover 12 and 34 nodes of a 13,998-entry tree. Files like gstquery.c, gstevent.c and gstbuffer.c are real and load-bearing; they are context, not nodes.
  • The elements walked (fakesrc, identity, capsfilter, queue, typefind, fakesink) are the core’s own test-grade elements — chosen because their behavior is fully visible without external plugins. Real decoders live elsewhere and add their own negotiation quirks.
  • No benchmarks are claimed: the sources show mechanics, not performance. Unit tests under subprojects/gstreamer/tests/check/gst/ (including one for gstpad.c) are the best executable documentation of these behaviors.
  • To see these concepts driven by a finished consumer rather than test elements, read our mpv source tour — a player that does the same state-and-buffer dance with its own graph.
entry.summary: What happens between gst-launch and the first buffer: a line-linked tour through gstpad.c, gstbin.c, gstcaps.c and the bus, on the current main branch of the GStreamer monorepo.

entry.title: HandBrake source tour: the state machine behind “2 hours remaining”

link.title: HandBrake source tour: the state machine behind “2 hours remaining”

entry.content:
Your movie is forty minutes in and HandBrake confidently displays “2 hours remaining.” You pause to grab coffee, hit resume, and the estimate keeps being roughly right — which should raise an eyebrow, because nothing in that dialog looks like it could know the future. The number is not produced by the GUI at all. The graphical frontends merely read a shared state struct; the arithmetic lives in libhb, the C engine underneath, in one function that divides remaining frames by a rolling average of measured encoding speed. Once you know that, the ETA stops being a promise and becomes what it really is: a sliding-window measurement with a model of the work attached.

The rest of the interface behaves the same way. “Scanning…” is a formula over title and preview counts, not a progress bar someone drew. Pause for ten minutes and the ETA does not drift ten minutes into the future, because the resume path explicitly credits the paused time against the average-speed math. Cancelling is not a graceful shutdown either — it is one boolean flag that every worker thread polls between buffers. These are the design decisions of a library that treats the whole encode as one measurable flow, and they are all visible in the source.

That flow is the actual architecture. Every encode is an hb_job_t record that gets expanded into a chain of worker threads, each linked to the next by small fixed-capacity frame queues called fifos. A reader demuxes packets, libavcodec decoders turn them into frames, a sync stage re-aligns audio and video on timestamps, filters run, an encoder compresses, a muxer writes the file — and every one of those stages is the same struct with three function pointers, running as its own pthread. This tour walks master (we checked it at commit e2dd8d8, November 2026) the way a frame would travel. One drift note up front: older guides cite libhb/job.c, but that file no longer exists — the job struct now lives in a shared header, as noted below.

The libhb core at a glance: the public API and its state machine on the left, the title scan feeding the work chain in the middle, the FFmpeg codec layer doing the heavy lifting, and the muxer publishing WORKDONE on the right.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • Everything starts in hb_init, L207, which allocates the hb_handle_t, sets HB_STATE_IDLE, and starts the library’s own monitor thread named “libhb”.
  • Scanning is requested through hb_scan, L377, which defaults to 10 previews (L424) and short-circuits if the same source was already scanned.
  • The scan thread’s body is ScanFunc, L140, which probes each title with DecodePreviews, L760.
  • When you press Start, hb_start, L1995 flips state to HB_STATE_WORKING and calls hb_work_init at L2019 to spawn the work thread.
  • The wiring happens in do_job, L1716, which sizes the job’s fifos and chains reader, decoders, sync, filters, encoder, and muxer into job->list_work.
  • Each worker then lives inside hb_work_loop, L2422: block on an incoming fifo, run the stage, push results downstream.
  • Video pixels go through hb_decavcodecv, L2201, the libavcodec wrapper that drives avcodec_send_packet and avcodec_receive_frame at L1420 and L1430.
  • Finished packets drain into hb_muxer, L770, and the monitor thread publishes HB_STATE_WORKDONE at L2306 when the work thread exits.

The detail view: API core and monitor thread on the left, the state-and-ETA machinery at the top, job wiring and fifo transport in the middle, and the scan, decode, filter, and encode-mux stages filling the right.

The state machine behind “2 hours remaining”

All progress reporting hangs off one bitmask. The states — idle, scanning, scandone, working, paused, workdone, muxing, searching — are defined at HB_STATE_*, L1469, and the working state carries the fields the UI cares about, including eta_seconds at L1505. The frontend polls hb_get_state, L2092, which copies the struct under a lock and demotes one-shot states like WORKDONE back to IDLE so the next read is clean.

The ETA math itself sits in the sync stage: UpdateState, L3242. Progress is simply frame_count / est_frame_count (L3274). The current speed comes from a four-sample sliding window over the last second (L3279), and after a four-second warm-up the average speed is measured since encode start, corrected by st_paused — the paused-time counter that hb_resume, L2045 credits at L2056. Then comes the whole promise: eta = remaining_frames / rate_avg, split into hours, minutes, and seconds at L3287. JSON API consumers get the same values as ETASeconds at L89.

Denominator honesty is the interesting part. est_frame_count is itself an estimate derived from title duration and frame rate (L2372), so a variable-frame-rate source makes the estimate move during the run. The whole machine is supervised by the monitor thread thread_func, L2255, which wakes every 50 ms (L2317), notices when the scan or work thread has exited, and publishes SCANDONE (L2294) or WORKDONE. That is the same pattern we saw in the OBS Studio tour, where a monitor thread also owns lifecycle transitions — but HandBrake’s loops are throughput-driven rather than racing a 33 ms deadline.

One job, many threads: the work chain

The work thread starts in work_func, L107, which pops jobs from the handle’s queue, expands JSON jobs and multi-pass encodes into a pass list, and calls do_job once per pass. Then do_job, L1716 does the real wiring. It creates the job’s frame queues — the sizes are honest constants at L40-46: 16 entries for small queues, 32 for large, 4 for mini queues between filters, and 65536 for the deliberately unbounded subtitle queues. Every worker is an instance of the struct at hb_work_object_s, L1554: init/work/close entry points, fifo_in/fifo_out, and shared done/die flags.

The chain is assembled in plain sequence: the video decoder gets job->fifo_in and outputs to fifo_raw (L2012), the sync work object follows (L2025), each video filter is chained with mini-fifos ending in fifo_render (L2150), the encoder consumes that (L2173), and the muxer is added last (L2201). Init is called for every object (L2216), then one thread per stage is launched via hb_thread_init at L2233 — a thin pthread wrapper at L1021 alongside the hb_lock/hb_yield portability layer. The loop at hb_work_loop, L2422 blocks on hb_fifo_get_wait (L1269), invokes the stage, and pushes via hb_fifo_push (L1436) — sleeping whenever the downstream fifo is full, which is how backpressure throttles the reader automatically. Filters run the same loop shape in filter_loop, L2506.

If you like this composition style, it is a cousin of the GStreamer element model — but HandBrake ships its own tiny scheduler instead of a framework, and the coupling is deliberately simple: queues, not signals.

Where ffmpeg actually runs

The heavy lifting is libavcodec, wrapped, not forked. Decoding lives in hb_decavcodecv, L2201 (“Video decoder (libavcodec)”) and the audio twin hb_decavcodeca, L66; the per-packet path is decodePacket (L1763) feeding the canonical avcodec_send_packet/avcodec_receive_frame pair. On the output side, hb_encavcodec, L83 covers MPEG-2/4, VP8/9, and every hardware path — NVENC, VAAPI, AMD VCE, MediaFoundation, Intel QSV are all selected inside encavcodecInit, L349. The specialist encoders x264, x265, and SVT-AV1 get their own wrapper files and are registered alongside at L2194 during hb_global_init, L2153.

Filters are two-layered. Named HandBrake filters — deinterlacing via hb_filter_decomb, L182, geometry via hb_filter_crop_scale, L27 — are built by the factory hb_filter_init, L5628. Arbitrary FFmpeg filter graphs are supported too: hb_avfilter_graph_init, L39 allocates an AVFilterGraph and parses user strings, which is how the command-line --vf avfilter syntax reaches libavfilter. For a deeper map of that library itself, read our FFmpeg source tour; the difference here is intent — HandBrake uses libav* as a codec engine while keeping the flow control, timestamps, and quality decisions in its own work chain.

Scan: the price of admission

Before any encode, the “scan” thread earns the progress bar you see when you open a source. hb_scan_init, L89 clamps the preview count to a minimum of 3 (L114-116), sets HB_STATE_SCANNING at L128, and starts ScanFunc, L140. Per title it calls DecodePreviews, L760, which decodes sample frames spread through the stream to detect crop values, audio properties, and subtitles — the scan reuses the very same libavcodec decoder objects as the real encode, which is a neat economy. Scan progress is its own formula in UpdateState3, L2055: a title-phase component plus a preview-phase component, weighted half and half across the two phases (L2064-2066).

From configure.py to hb.dll

The build has a few quirks worth knowing before you try it. The top-level configure is not an autoconf script at all — it is a 24-line POSIX shell shim that hunts for any Python 3 interpreter and execs make/configure.py (L15-21). Third-party libraries are built from source into a contrib/ prefix; the dependency list for libhb alone (L1-4) reads like a codec hall of fame: FFMPEG, X264, X265, SVT-AV1, LIBVPX, LIBDAV1D, LIBBLURAY, LIBDVDREAD, LIBDVDNAV, FDKAAC, LIBVPL for QSV, LIBDOVI, LIBUDFREAD, and friends. Platform divergence is handled in one make fragment: MinGW builds link a hb.dll plus import library (L115), while macOS compiles Objective-C sources and Metal shaders per L70-72.

Tree shape, measured on this checkout: libhb/ holds 85 top-level C files with 42 headers under libhb/handbrake/; GUIs live in gtk/, macosx/, and win/; the CLI is test/test.c; .github, pkg/, scripts/, graphics/, and preset/ round out the root. The drift we promised: there is no libhb/job.c — struct hb_job_s moved to common.h, L671 with setters like hb_job_set_encoder_preset in common.c, and any tutorial citing the old path will dead-end. Finally, master sits just after the 1.11.x series: NEWS.markdown tops out at 1.12.0, which adds Deband and BM3D video filters, a batch of audio filters (declick, declip, compressor), and marks AMD hardware decoding experimental.

Honest Limits

  • The ETA is only as good as its denominator: est_frame_count comes from duration times assumed frame rate, so variable-frame-rate sources will make the estimate visibly revise itself mid-run.
  • In the first four seconds of a pass the progress fields are deliberately unset — UpdateState refuses to guess before the warm-up window (L3281-3307).
  • Scan decisions are preview-based by design: with as few as 3 previews per title, detected crop, audio, and subtitle choices can differ from what a full decode would find.
  • Subtitle fifos are explicitly unbounded (65536 entries at L1991) with a comment explaining the deadlock that forces it — memory growth there is accepted, not impossible.
  • This tour maps the master branch at commit e2dd8d8e1ac0 (November 2026); libhb reorganizes occasionally, so line numbers will drift even when symbols survive.
  • We traced structure and control flow, not codec quality: the hardware encoder paths are cited at their entry points, and their real behavior depends on your drivers and silicon.
entry.summary: A guided walk through HandBrake's libhb core in C: the HB_STATE_* machine, the fifo-coupled work chain where every encode is an hb_job_t, and the exact lines that compute the ETA you watch while a movie transcodes.

entry.title: Inside ImageMagick 7: A Source Tour of the Pixel Cache, the Coder Registry and the magick CLI

link.title: Inside ImageMagick 7: A Source Tour of the Pixel Cache, the Coder Registry and the magick CLI

entry.content:
Type magick img.png -resize 50% out.jpg and it finishes before you lift your finger off the Enter key. One hundred milliseconds of work, it seems, for a program whose binary drags in a delegate list, a dozen format libraries and a resource-management subsystem. That speed is not an accident: the command line you typed was decomposed into a strict sequence of registry lookups and cache decisions, and one of those decisions silently picks between RAM and a temporary file on disk.

The hidden cast is worth naming. A single resize touches three separate registries: the coder registry in MagickCore/magick.c, which decides that img.png is decoded by the PNG coder and out.jpg by the JPEG coder; delegates.xml, the list of external programs ImageMagick will shell out to when no built-in coder exists; and the resource budgets in MagickCore/resource.c, which decide whether your pixels sit in an anonymous memory block, a file-backed mapping, or a seekable scratch file. Get one of these wrong and you either get NoDecodeDelegateForThisImageFormat errors or a machine that starts thrashing on a 500-megapixel TIFF.

This tour follows the exact path that one command takes through the sources on the main branch, with every claim linked to a specific line so you can click through and argue with it. If you enjoy this kind of archaeology, our FFmpeg transcode internals tour, the HandBrake encoder walkthrough, and the LÖVE2D Lua runtime look cover neighboring media engines from the same angle.

The whole flow on main: main() hands argv to the wand layer, options dispatch in the order you typed them, filenames trigger reads and writes through the coder registry, and every pixel lands in the pixel cache that OpenPixelCache() allocates. Each node maps to a real file in the repository.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • main() is a thin shell. main, L191 forwards to MagickMain() (L62), which calls MagickCommandGenesis() (L162) — the binary itself contains almost no logic.
  • The CLI boots and parses in one place. MagickCommandGenesis, L117 sets up the MagickCLI environment, then ProcessCommandOptions, L588 walks argv one token at a time.
  • Options run in the order you typed them. CLIOption, L5398 classifies each option — setting, operator, or no-image operation — and executes it immediately; there is no two-pass collection of options.
  • A filename argument is just the read option. operation.c, L4957 turns it into ReadImages(), which funnels into ReadImage() (constitute.c, L998).
  • Format resolution happens before any pixels move. ReadImage() calls SetImageInfo() (L653) to sniff the format, then GetMagickInfo() (L660) to find the registered coder.
  • The decoder is a function pointer, not a switch. decoder() call, L730 invokes whatever handler GetImageDecoder() returned — for our command that is ReadPNGImage, L3918 for the input.
  • -resize is one option among hundreds. operation.c, L3274 matches the string, parses the geometry, and calls ResizeImage() (resize.c, L3820).
  • Writing mirrors reading. The write option (operation.c, L4984) calls WriteImages(), and WriteImage() (constitute.c, L1291) looks up an encoder the same way and calls it at L1499 — landing in the JPEG coder.
  • Every pixel of every stage lives in the cache. OpenPixelCache, L3783 allocates the backing storage for all of it, and its type decision is the subject of the last section.

The detail view: 34 functions across eight groups, following img.png from argv to the JPEG encoder, including the delegate fallback, the resource-accounted cache type selection, and the two-pass resampling inside ResizeImage().

The option loop is the program

There is no planner. ImageMagick executes your command strictly left to right: each token is dispatched by CLIOption() the moment it is read, so magick a.png -resize 50% b.jpg reads a.png, resizes, then writes b.jpg — while magick a.png b.jpg -resize 50% resizes after writing. Options split into classes handled by different functions: settings go to CLISettingOptionInfo() (operation.c, L427), and options that need no existing image — read, write, clone — go to CLINoImageOperator() (L4874).

Settings live on two levels. Global options sit on struct _ImageInfo (image.h, L358); per-image state sits on struct _Image (L131) with its columns and rows at L152. A fresh Image is born through AcquireImage() (image.c, L136), which seeds every field from the ImageInfo defaults, and SyncImageSettings() (image.c, L4086, declared at image.h, L533) copies the global settings onto each image later — which is how -quality 90 reaches the JPEG encoder even though you typed it before the filename. Operators like -resize do not mutate the source image: they get a fresh one via CloneImage() (image.c, L801), which is also why the image list behaves like an undo stack.

The registry decides who touches your pixels

ReadImage() is a dispatcher around a function pointer. After SetImageInfo() resolves the format from the filename or magic bytes, GetMagickInfo() (magick.c, L605) finds the MagickInfo record that each coder registered at load time via RegisterMagickInfo() (L1712). The handler comes from GetImageDecoder() (L217) and is invoked directly at constitute.c, L730 — the PNG and JPEG coders are just two of the hundred-plus files in coders/, each exporting a ReadXXXImage/WriteXXXImage pair.

If no built-in coder claims the format, the delegate list gets its turn. ReadImage() falls back to GetDelegateInfo() (constitute.c, L736), which consults the command table loaded from delegates.xml (delegate.c, L93); a hit sends the request to InvokeDelegate() (delegate.c, L1745), which expands the format string into a shell command and executes it through ExternalDelegateCommand() (L393, called at L1926). When the external program finishes, ReadImage() re-sniffs the temporary file and enters the normal coder path. The write side is the exact mirror: GetImageEncoder() (magick.c, L247) produces the handler whose call at constitute.c, L1499 lands in WriteJPEGImage() (jpeg.c, L3672) or WritePNGImage() (png.c, L11671).

One more gate sits in front of both calls, and it is easy to miss: a policy check. Before the decoder runs, IsCoderAuthorized() is consulted with ReadPolicyRights (constitute.c, L726); the encoder side repeats the check with WritePolicyRights at L1496. This is how a policy.xml rule can refuse to decode, say, PDF or MVG entirely — the handler lookup succeeds, and the policy layer simply vetoes the call. It also explains those baffling “not authorized” errors that appear after upgrading a system image: the coder is present, the delegate is fine, but a security policy shipped in the package has the format disabled.

Why huge images go to disk

Every operator reaches pixels through the same door: GetImagePixelCache() (cache.c, L1773) returns the cache attached to an Image, allocating it first if needed. The allocation itself was set up by AcquirePixelCache() (L195), and the storage type is chosen inside OpenPixelCache() by asking the resource manager first: AcquireMagickResource(AreaResource, ...) checks the image area against configured limits (L3911), and then AcquireMagickResource() (resource.c, L187) arbitrates memory, map and disk budgets in that order.

The ladder looks like this. If the area fits and MemoryResource allows, the pixels go into an anonymous memory block or heap allocation and the cache type becomes MemoryCache (cache.c, L3949). If memory is exhausted but map resources remain, the cache is written to a scratch file and mmap-ed back as MapCache (L4128). If even that fails, the type becomes DiskCache (L4106) — every pixel access becomes a seek-and-read against the scratch file, which is precisely why a 500-megapixel panorama still resizes on a laptop with 8 GB of RAM, just slowly. There is even a fourth rung: if a cache:hosts registry entry names a remote server, the pixels go to a DistributedCache (L4016) on another machine.

The resize itself never knows the difference. ResizeImage() acquires a filter (resize.c, L3878) and runs two separable passes, HorizontalFilter() (L3339) then VerticalFilter() (L3581), each pulling pixels through the same cache accessors — GetAuthenticPixels() (cache.c, L1562) for regions the operator will write back, and the virtual-pixel variants for reading beyond the edges when a filter kernel overhangs the border. Because every access funnels through the nexus layer, the identical filter code runs whether the cache happens to be RAM, a file mapping, or a seek loop over a scratch file; the strategy is a property of the cache, not of the operation. That separation is the quiet architectural win of MagickCore: operators are written once, and the disk-thrashing fallback costs you latency instead of correctness.

From ImageMagick 6’s convert to ImageMagick 7’s magick

Several layout facts surprised us while walking this tree. The old IM6 layout — a magick/ core plus a wand/ library plus a monolithic convert.c CLI — is gone: IM7 splits the sources into MagickCore/ (the engine), MagickWand/ (the C API and the CLI, with operation.c alone carrying the option table), Magick++/ and coders/. There is no MagickCore/convert.c. The legacy convert name survives only as one entry in a command table at utilities/magick.c, L87, mapping to ConvertImageCommand() — which now lives in MagickWand/deprecate.c (L498), a file whose name tells you exactly how the maintainers feel about it. All of these commands, magick, convert, mogrify and the rest, dispatch through the same MagickCommandGenesis() loop (L162); the old behaviors are option-table entries, not a second parser.

The build reflects the same philosophy of optional everything. Version numbers live in m4/version.m4 (7.1.2 with patchlevel 36, marked beta, at L27-L31) and are pulled into configure.ac with a single m4_include (L25). Every heavy delegate is a configure switch: --without-jpeg (Install-unix.txt, L325), --without-freetype (L316), and Ghostscript documented as a prerequisite for the whole EPS/PS family (L431). Even delegates.xml is a template whose external program names get substituted at build time (L253), so the paths baked into your binary match the machine that compiled it. Two quirks from our own clone: the default branch is main, not master, and a sparse checkout of MagickCore, MagickWand, coders and utilities covers a surprisingly small slice — about 1,890 tracked paths in total.

Honest Limits

  • This tour covers the C core only. The Magick++/ C++ bindings and PerlMagick/ are separate APIs over the same engine and were not traced.
  • The DistributedCache path at cache.c, L4016 requires running ImageMagick’s separate cache server process; we verified the code path but never exercised it.
  • Delegate quality is out of scope: when ExternalDelegateCommand() shells out to Ghostscript or similar, the result depends on that external program, not on this repository.
  • All line numbers refer to commit fd4c374db74a on main (dated 2026-11-12). ImageMagick moves fast; expect drift in the coders, which are actively patched for security.
  • We did not audit IM6-versus-IM7 option compatibility. The claim that convert is an alias rests on this repo’s sources alone — the IM6 tree, where the old parser lived, is not part of this codebase.
entry.summary: What one magick command really does: a line-linked tour through MagickCore's pixel cache, the coder registry in magick.c, delegates.xml shell-outs and the MagickWand option loop on the main branch.

entry.title: Inside Jellyfin: What Happens in the Ten Seconds After You Press Play

link.title: Inside Jellyfin: What Happens in the Ten Seconds After You Press Play

entry.content:
You press play on a 4K HEVC movie. Your TV’s decoder flips through the profile level, chokes, and silently reports back that it can’t handle it. Four seconds later a green-ish CPU graph on your server box says one core is pegged, and the picture arrives anyway. Between those two moments, Jellyfin has negotiated client capabilities, decided that direct play is dead, generated an ffmpeg command line roughly a screenful long, spawned a child process, registered it in a job table, and told the client which manifest URL to poll. Nothing about that sequence is magic — it is a handful of C# classes in a repo you can read in an afternoon.

This is a tour of that code. Jellyfin’s server is a .NET application in the classic layered shape: Jellyfin.Server boots the process, Jellyfin.Api exposes the HTTP surface, Emby.Server.Implementations holds the heavy machinery, and MediaBrowser.Controller defines the contracts everything else codes against. Everything below is pinned to the master branch at commit 218514ab6bab, and every symbol and line number was read from the actual tree rather than from memory. If you have ever wondered what a media server looks like when it is not a monolith blob but a layered .NET solution, this is your map.

We follow one thread all the way down: the play request. Two architecture diagrams were generated from the live tree — an overview of the five subsystems involved, and a detail map of the transcode path. If you came from the Kodi side of things, Kodi’s source tour covers the client half of the same conversation; this one covers the server that answers it.

Overview: how a play request crosses the host bootstrap, the HTTP layer, the library item graph, session tracking, and the ffmpeg engine. Rendered from the master tree.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • Program.Main, L72 parses command-line options and hands off to StartApp, which creates application paths, wires logging, and runs migrations before any HTTP listener exists (L170 is where CoreAppHost is constructed).
  • ApplicationHost.RegisterServices, L499 fills the dependency-injection container with the singletons that define the whole system: IMediaEncoder at L567, ILibraryManager at L577, ISessionManager at L608.
  • Startup.ConfigureServices, L64 calls AddJellyfinApi with the API plugin assemblies, and MapControllers, L250 is where every controller below becomes a route.
  • MediaEncoder.SetFFmpegPath, L180 resolves ffmpeg through three fallbacks — the --ffmpeg switch, encoding.xml, then the system PATH at L200 — and interrogates the binary for its available encoders, decoders, filters, and hardware accelerators at L226.
  • VideosController.GetVideoStream, L318 maps dozens of query parameters into a typed request and checks at L442 whether a static, no-transcode response can be served.
  • DynamicHlsController.GetMasterHlsVideoPlaylist, L408 handles the master.m3u8 route declared at L404 — the entry point of every adaptive playback that needs transcoding.
  • SessionManager.OnPlaybackStart, L765 records that a client actually began playing, storing state in a ConcurrentDictionary at L64.
  • LibraryManager.GetItemById, L1689 is the workhorse lookup behind almost every controller call; the class itself implements ILibraryManager at L64.
  • TranscodeManager.StartFfMpeg, L371 is the last stop: permission checks, then a raw System.Diagnostics.Process whose FileName is the validated encoder path at L430.

Detail: the transcode path end to end — request DTOs, state assembly, argument building, the spawned ffmpeg job, and the helpers that throttle and clean up after it.

Two-phase startup: migrations before Kestrel

The boot sequence is stricter than most .NET servers you will have seen. Program.StartApp runs ApplyStartupMigrationAsync before the web host is even built, and a separate setup server keeps the first-run wizard alive while the main one is still starting (L143). Only after appHost.InitializeServices (L222) and the migration stages complete does _jellyfinHost.StartAsync() bring Kestrel up — and if the bind fails you get the delightfully blunt log line “Kestrel failed to start!” at L247.

One detail worth stealing for your own .NET work: the generic host is created with Host.CreateDefaultBuilder (L178), but ASP.NET does not accept a custom service collection, so the code explicitly re-binds appHost.ServiceProvider = _jellyfinHost.Services (L202). The hand-rolled DI container and the framework one are the same object; there is no duplication. If you are more familiar with how Django organizes configuration, note the contrast: Jellyfin pushes almost all decisions into singletons resolved through one container, whereas Django leans on settings modules and signals. Same problem — where does configuration live — different institutions.

ffmpeg validation happens inside that startup phase, not lazily at first playback. ApplicationHost L429 calls SetFFmpegPath() and throws FfmpegException("Failed to find valid ffmpeg") at L433 if the binary does not pass muster. A media server that cannot transcode is a file share, so the refusal is at boot, by design.

The item graph: everything is a BaseItem

The library is a graph of entities rooted at BaseItem, L45 — a 3,145-line abstract class that supplies provider IDs, metadata hooks, and access checks. Video, L30 extends it for movie-shaped things and tracks a PrimaryVersionId so alternate editions can point at a canonical one. Containers extend it too: Folder.GetChildren, L1516 returns typed child lists that the browsing API consumes.

LibraryManager is the facade over that graph. RegisterItem at L325 inserts resolved entities into the live cache, ResolveItem at L766 decides what kind of item a discovered file is, and ValidateMediaLibrary at L1403 is the scheduled sweep that reconciles disk and database. Browsing requests ride the same object: ItemsController.GetItems at L173 builds an InternalItemsQuery, and for folder traversal falls through to folder.GetItems(query) at L595, which the comments there note applies user-access filtering server-side. Security is a property of the query, not of the endpoint.

Sessions and the playback event bus

SessionManager, L49 is where “who is watching what right now” lives. Its _activeConnections dictionary at L64 maps connection IDs to SessionInfo records, each of which carries a NowPlayingItem and a live TranscodingInfo. Clients report progress through routes like Sessions/{id}/Playing, L119, and remote-control commands flow the other way through SendPlayCommand at L143.

The events matter more than the storage. PlaybackStart, PlaybackProgress, and PlaybackStopped are declared at L127 and friends, and — the part that surprised me — TranscodeManager subscribes to them, L95. The transcode engine learns about playback state by listening, not by being called. That inversion is what keeps the subsystems loosely coupled: a client that stops reporting progress eventually starves its job of active requests, and the cleanup path takes over.

The four-second fallback: from PlaybackInfo to an ffmpeg worker

Now the thread you came for. When the client’s player opens the item it first POSTs to PlaybackInfo, L116, passing its DeviceProfile — the machine-readable list of codecs and profiles it can decode. The server answers with MediaSourceInfo objects annotated with TranscodeReasons. A 4K HEVC Main10 stream against a profile that only promises 8-bit H.264 gets flagged, and the client requests master.m3u8 instead of the raw file.

Inside DynamicHlsController, the handler locks on the playlist path (LockAsync — concurrent clients asking for the same item do not race), and only if the playlist does not yet exist calls StartFfMpeg, L309. Before any process is born, AcquireResources, L383 checks the user’s EnableVideoPlaybackTranscoding permission at L388 — a user without it gets a clean refusal, not a busy server. The Process object is constructed at L417 with stderr redirected (the comment there warns both pipes must be consumed or ffmpeg deadlocks), and the job is registered via OnTranscodeBeginning at L438. The controller then waits for the first few segments (WaitForMinimumSegmentCount at L328) before returning the manifest, which is why the pause before playback feels deliberate.

The argument string itself is assembled by EncodingHelper, L34, a partial class of thousands of lines that picks video encoders, hardware acceleration flags, and subtitle burn-in parameters from the interrogated capability lists captured at startup. Each live worker is a TranscodingJob, L13 holding its Process handle at L65, plus an ActiveRequestCount — the counter that makes orphaned jobs killable. Two helpers keep long sessions sane: a TranscodingThrottler, L14 that pauses ffmpeg when the client’s buffer is ahead, and a TranscodingSegmentCleaner, L17 that deletes already-played segments. If you want the deeper mechanics of the binary being driven here, the ffmpeg tour dissects the command-line vocabulary this helper speaks.

From global.json to Jellyfin.slnx

A few facts about building this thing, straight from the tree:

  • Toolchain: global.json pins SDK 10.0.0 with rollForward: latestMinor — Jellyfin master is already on .NET 10 previews while SharedVersion.cs carries AssemblyVersion 13.0.0.
  • Solution format: the root solution is Jellyfin.slnx — the XML-based solution format — referencing 43 .csproj projects; there is no classic .sln anywhere in the tree.
  • Package management: all 82 NuGet versions are centralized in Directory.Packages.props, so transitive version drift across projects is structurally impossible.
  • Hygiene: a BannedSymbols.txt file feeds an analyzer that blocks forbidden APIs, and the repo ships dedicated fuzz/ projects (Jellyfin.Api.Fuzz, Emby.Server.Implementations.Fuzz) targeting the parsers most exposed to hostile media metadata.
  • Source generators: MediaEncoder is a partial class using a generated Regex (FfprobePathRegex() at L172) — the logging and regex hot paths use compile-time generation rather than runtime parsing.

Honest Limits

  • This tour reads master at one commit (218514ab6bab); all line numbers are valid for that snapshot and will drift. The repository moves fast.
