  • No server was run during this tour. The play-request flow is derived by reading code paths, not by profiling a live transcode; the “four seconds” in the intro is narrative framing, not a benchmark from this repo.
  • The web UI is a separate repository (jellyfin-web). Program.cs only validates the hosted web content path at L120 and suggests --nowebclient otherwise; nothing about the dashboard’s internals can be concluded from this tree.
  • TranscodeManager exposes more job-lifecycle machinery than covered here (per-job cancellation, KillTranscodingJobs at L194, live-TV job variants). The claim “one ffmpeg process per playlist path, serialized by a lock” is verified; deeper concurrency guarantees under many simultaneous sessions were not audited.
  • Hardware-acceleration behavior depends on what EncoderValidator discovers on your machine at startup; this tour cannot tell you which GPU feature flags your box will produce.
entry.summary: A source tour of Jellyfin's C#/.NET media server on master: the ASP.NET Core host, the LibraryManager item graph, session tracking, and the TranscodeManager that schedules ffmpeg workers.

entry.title: Inside Kodi’s application loop: one thread renders the skin while a 50 GB remux decodes underneath

link.title: Inside Kodi’s application loop: one thread renders the skin while a 50 GB remux decodes underneath

entry.content:
A Raspberry Pi 4 is playing a 50 GB remux — HEVC, 4K, a full bitstream at 40 Mbps — and at the same time you arrow down through its skin menus at 60 fps with animations that never hitch. If you have ever written a player yourself, you know how unnatural that is: decode work that overruns its slot should stall the frame pump, and any GUI sharing the process should stutter the moment the disk hiccups. Kodi does this with one C++ process and no scheduler service, which raises the question every reader of its source eventually asks: who exactly owns which thread?

The answer is a surprisingly rigid contract. There is one main loop — CApplication::Run() — that owns the graphics context, the input devices, and the skin, and it never blocks on playback. Playback is delegated to a small family of threads (VideoPlayer, plus one video_thread and one audio thread per stream), each of which has its own message queue and its own idea of time. The two worlds only touch in narrow, deliberate places. If you have read our FFmpeg tour, most of the decode side will look familiar; the novelty is the coordination layer above it.

The third tenant is the strangest: Python addons live inside this same process. A scraped-metadata script and a GUI widget pack both execute as CPython interpreters embedded in the media center, and they are never allowed to touch the GUI thread directly — they post messages, and once per frame the loop opens a measured 2–10 ms window with the graphics lock dropped so pending Python calls can squeeze through. Where a single-threaded runtime like LÖVE2D gives you callbacks and no threads at all, Kodi gives you threads but fences them off. And the interpreter setup is not the default CPython embedding pattern either — Kodi runs each script in its own sub-interpreter. Let’s walk the whole machine, top to bottom.

Overview of Kodi's architecture: one CApplication::Run() iteration pumps Process, FrameMove and Render on the GUI thread, while the VideoPlayer thread family and its ffmpeg demuxer/codec layer advance independently and meet the loop only at message queues.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • Everything begins at main, L40, which installs signal handlers that only set an atomic quit flag, then calls XBMC_Run, L22 — a fixed bootstrap of Create(), CreateGUI(), Initialize() and finally the blocking Run() (L26, L63).
  • CApplication::Create, L255 registers the service registry before any window exists, and even initializes ffmpeg’s network layer there: avformat_network_init() sits at L320.
  • The heart is CApplication::Run, L1441: while (!m_bStop) RunIteration(); — nothing more. Every subsystem is serviced from inside RunIteration, L1469, which calls Process() (L1474), FrameMove(true, renderGUI) (L1479) and Render() (L1484) in that order, on the same thread, every cycle.
  • CApplication::Process, L2216 is the intake valve: it dispatches messages other threads posted to windows (L2219), lets script threads shut down cleanly (L2234), and drains the application messenger (L2240); slow housekeeping runs every 500 ms via ProcessSlow (L2248).
  • CApplication::FrameMove, L1328 processes input through CInputManager::Process() (L1354) and then opens the external-call door described below (L1362).
  • CApplication::Render, L896 draws the GUI layer through GetWindowManager().Render() (L939) and only then the video layer via RenderEx() (L951).
  • Playback starts through the facade CApplicationPlayer::OpenFile, L107, whose player was built by CreatePlayer, L87 from the core factory — the chosen implementation is CVideoPlayer, whose own pump runs at CVideoPlayer::Process, L1623 on a dedicated thread.
  • Below that, the ffmpeg layer does the real work: the container is opened by CDVDDemuxFFmpeg::Open, L253, packets are pulled by CDVDDemuxFFmpeg::Read, L1365, and the codec is created by CDVDVideoCodecFFmpeg::Open, L330.

The detail view expands each stage: the bootstrap chain, the three-phase main loop, the window manager and input path, the Python sub-interpreter setup, the VideoPlayer state machine with its per-stream threads, and the ffmpeg demux/decode path feeding the render manager.

One thread owns the frame

The main thread is the only thread that ever touches the skin. RunIteration is a straight line — process messages, move the GUI, draw the GUI — and the rhythm is enforced locally. When renderGUI is false (headless or background operation), the loop sleeps up to 15 ms per iteration, with a comment that reads Simulates ~66fps at L1488; when a GUI is present, there is no sleep at all and the loop runs as fast as the render system allows. The window manager’s side of the bargain is CGUIWindowManager::Process, L1287 for animation advance and CGUIWindowManager::Render, L1429 for drawing, both invoked only from the loop above.

Cross-thread traffic is funneled into a single queue. Any thread can post a TMSG_* message via the application messenger, but only CApplicationMessenger::ProcessMessages, L203, called from the loop, ever executes the payloads. This is the mechanism behind every “please do something on the GUI thread” in the codebase — play requests, volume changes, dialog opens — and it is why playback never takes a lock the GUI needs.

The VideoPlayer thread family

When you press play, the item crosses one boundary — from the app facade into the player core — and from then on belongs to another thread. CVideoPlayer is constructed as CThread("VideoPlayer") at L763, and its constructor immediately builds the per-stream engines in CreatePlayers, L728: a CVideoPlayerVideo (L733), a CVideoPlayerAudio (L736), plus subtitle, teletext, RDS and ID3 carriers. Each engine is itself a thread with a message queue.

The player’s pump is a state machine that re-evaluates its own wiring every pass. CVideoPlayer::Process, L1623 loops on while (!m_bAbortRequest), and each iteration checks whether it needs to (re)open the input stream (L1657), (re)open the demuxer (L1673), or auto-select default tracks (L1686). Commands from the GUI — seeks, pauses, stream switches — are not calls but messages, consumed by HandleMessages, L3179 once per pass. That is the whole trick behind responsive seeking: the GUI thread posts, the player thread disposes.

Packets then fan out. ReadPacket, L1243 pulls from the demuxer, and the loop routes each packet by stream type — ProcessVideoData at L2036 hands it to the video engine’s queue. Backpressure is explicit: the loop refuses to read more when m_VideoPlayerVideo->AcceptsData() is false (L1720), so a slow decoder stalls the demux pump instead of growing memory without bound. The video engine lives in its own loop at CVideoPlayerVideo::Process, L326 — it logs running thread: video_thread, waits on GetMessage() (L362), decodes, and pushes finished pictures out via OutputPicture (L378). The audio side mirrors it at CVideoPlayerAudio::Process, L232.

From DemuxPacket to a picture

The decode path is a thin veneer over ffmpeg. The demuxer wrapper opens the container with avformat_open_input() (L308) and avformat_find_stream_info() (L603) — the latter is why a big remux sometimes takes a visible beat before the first frame. When a video track is selected, CVideoPlayerVideo::OpenStream, L108 asks the factory for a codec (L140); CDVDFactoryCodec::CreateVideoCodec, L44 tries hardware paths first and falls back to software, where CDVDVideoCodecFFmpeg::Open, L330 runs the familiar sequence — avcodec_find_decoder (L369), avcodec_alloc_context3 (L380), avcodec_open2 (L448) — and its decode loop is the textbook pair avcodec_send_packet / avcodec_receive_frame (L644, L750). Audio repeats the same pattern in CVideoPlayerAudio::OpenStream, L82 with CreateAudioCodec at L91.

The last hop is deliberately lock-free-ish: decoded pictures land in the CRenderManager (Configure, L89; FrameMove, L288), a hand-off buffer the GUI thread’s RenderEx() pass consumes when it wants. The player thread never waits for the frame pump; the frame pump never waits for the player. On a Pi, that separation is what lets the skin animate at full rate while the HEVC decoder saturates its cores.

Python in a 2–10 ms window

The interpreter boots earlier than you’d expect: Py_Initialize() runs inside the XBPython constructor (L110), and the addon modules xbmc, xbmcaddon, xbmcdrm, xbmcgui, xbmcplugin, xbmcvfs are imported up front (L115). Each script then gets its own interpreter: CPythonInvoker::execute, L141 creates a thread state under Kodi’s main interpreter (L166) and calls Py_NewInterpreter() (L175) so one crashing addon does not poison the rest — a sub-interpreter design, not the naive single-GIL embedding. The bindings themselves are generated from SWIG interface files in xbmc/interfaces/swig/ (for example AddonModuleXbmcgui.i) over the hand-written API in xbmc/interfaces/legacy/.

The fences come in two forms. First, scripts cannot call GUI code from their own threads: the SWIG layer routes calls into messages that CApplication::Process, L2216 dispatches on the GUI thread. Second, when a Python call must complete synchronously, the main loop physically opens the door: inside FrameMove, L1328, if m_WaitingExternalCalls is set, the graphics lock is released and the loop sleeps a computed window — between 2 and 10 ms (up to 80 ms when nothing is playing) — before re-acquiring (L1365–L1377). That bounded gap, recomputed per frame, is the entire reason a slow Python addon makes menus laggy instead of frozen: it can only ever steal a slice, never the whole frame.

From bootstrap list to binary: build facts from this branch

Reading the tree itself tells you a lot about how this ships to fourteen platforms. The build is pure CMake — the root CMakeLists.txt, L1 demands cmake_minimum_required(VERSION 3.20), but Windows needs 3.30.6 (L3), and the project declares LANGUAGES CXX C ASM (L6) — the ASM is real, not cosmetic, since the codec path touches optimized primitives. The version file declares Kodi 23.0 ALPHA1 with addon API 22.90.701 (version.txt), so this branch is pre-release Omega-successor territory.

Two quirks stood out while cloning. First, the app class has moved: CApplication no longer lives at xbmc/Application.cpp as older forks and patches assume, but in xbmc/application/Application.cpp alongside its split handlers (ApplicationPlayer, ApplicationSkinHandling, ApplicationPowerHandling, …). If a third-party patch references the old path, it predates this. Second, there is a fourth platform main: xbmc/platform/wasm/main.cpp feeds an emscripten build, and the main loop handles it specially — CApplication::Run swaps its while loop for emscripten_set_main_loop under TARGET_WASM (L1453), and the Python layer sets PYTHONHOME into the Emscripten VFS at XBPython.cpp, L85. The repo root also carries AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md and .kodiai.yml — policy files for AI coding assistants, sitting next to sonar-project.properties and .clang-format. The SWIG dependency is vendored too: tools/depends/native/swig/ builds its own copy so the addon bindings stay reproducible.

Honest Limits

  • Everything here reflects commit 2c17cdd58fea (master, November 2026). Kodi reshuffles this code constantly — the Application.cpp move above is proof — so re-verify line numbers before citing them in a patch.
  • This tour traces the software decode path only. The hardware decoder classes in xbmc/cores/VideoPlayer/DVDCodecs/Video/ (DXVA, VAAPI, VDPAU, VTB, DRM PRIME, WebCodecs, Android MediaCodec) follow the same factory contract but were not traced line by line.
  • The 2–10 ms external-call window only exists when a Python addon is actively waiting (m_WaitingExternalCalls); a Python-free session never opens it, so the frame timing on a vanilla install is slightly different from what Section 4 describes.
  • The WASM/emscripten path was verified by reading code, not by building it; WasmRunIteration’s lifecycle depends on browser callbacks outside this repository.
  • ProcessSlow()’s 500 ms cadence and its screensaver/power checks are platform-gated in places; the exact behavior differs per target even though the call site is shared.

entry.title: Inside mpv’s playloop: the player core that skips frames instead of stuttering

link.title: Inside mpv’s playloop: the player core that skips frames instead of stuttering

entry.content:
Your video stalls for a tenth of a second, and most players respond by freezing the picture while the audio buffer runs dry — you get the ugly double-jerk of a paused frame followed by a sound hiccup. mpv almost never does this. When the machine cannot keep up, it quietly throws away frames that nobody would have seen anyway and keeps both the picture and the sound moving. That behavior is not an accident or a heuristic buried in a driver; it is the deliberate design of a very small amount of code in player/.

The second thing that surprises people is how old-school the architecture looks. There is one big C struct holding the whole player’s state, and one loop that ticks through it. There is no event framework, no actor system, no dependency injection — yet the demuxer, the decoders, the video output and the audio output all run as independent state machines that never block each other. If you enjoyed the decoder-centric tours of FFmpeg or the VLC playback core, this is the smaller, meaner cousin: same domain, radically fewer moving parts.

The third hook is the spacebar. You press it, the video freezes instantly — and when you press it again, sound resumes without a glitch even though the audio device has been sitting idle. The path between that keypress and the speaker runs through a dispatch queue, two handler functions, and a status variable called audio_status, and mpv’s authors have left comments along that path explaining exactly why each step exists. Let’s follow it.

Overview of mpv's playback architecture: one core thread runs run_playloop() forever, while the demuxer thread, the video-output thread and the audio device advance independently and wake the core when there is work to do.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • Everything starts at mpv_main, L455, which builds the central struct MPContext, L244 — a single struct holding tracks, playback statuses, timing fields and the dispatch queue the whole core sleeps on.
  • The outer lifetime loop is mp_play_files, L2280: an endless for(;;) that idles when there is nothing to play, loads the next playlist entry, then hands control to the per-file loop.
  • Per file, play_current_file, L1811 opens the demuxer and then simply spins run_playloop, L2111 until stop_play says otherwise — the actual implementation of run_playloop, L1326 lives in playloop.c and is about seventy lines of straight-line handler calls.
  • Each tick calls fill_audio_out_buffers, L1344 before write_video, L1345: audio is deliberately serviced first, because the audio device is the clock everything else follows.
  • The video side pulls packets via demux_read_packet_async, L2973, which never blocks: if the background reader has not caught up yet, the decoder just waits and the core stays responsive.
  • That background reader is demux_thread, L2746, a dedicated thread that keeps packet queues filled ahead of playback so the presentation loop never waits on disk or network.
  • Finished frames are handed to vo_thread, L1117, which schedules presentation against vertical sync and counts every frame it had to drop.
  • Finally the tick ends with mp_wait_events, L1385, where the core parks itself on a dispatch queue — it only spins again when a thread, a timeout, or your keyboard wakes it.

The detail view opens run_playloop() into its handlers and follows each thread: demuxer internals on one side, the video chain with its drop accounting, the audio chain with underrun recovery, and the command path from keypress to state change.

Pressing space: from keypress to silence

When you hit space, the core is almost certainly inside mp_wait_events, L53 — asleep on mp_dispatch_queue_process() with an effectively infinite deadline. The input thread does not touch player state directly; it queues a command, and the next run of mp_process_input, L110 drains that queue, calling run_command, L5954 for each. Pausing is handled by set_pause_state, L165, and this is where the design shows its seams deliberately: the function pushes the new state outward — ao_set_paused() to the audio device, vo_set_paused() to the video output — then calls mp_wakeup_core() so the loop re-runs and notices.

The subtle part is what is remembered. In the unpause branch, the code subtracts the wall-clock time spent paused from the frame timer ((void)get_relative_time(mpctx); // ignore time that passed during pause). The frame that was on screen when you paused is still exactly where it was; video and audio have not drifted, because nothing kept running. On resume, handle_playback_restart, L1157 flips the chain statuses back to STATUS_PLAYING and calls audio_start_ao, L1184 only after both chains report ready — that is the comment-level contract: “Actual playback starts when both audio and video are ready” (write_video, L1100). One keypress, one wakeup, one status flip; no timers racing, no leftover buffers to flush.

First playback has one more stop on the way. The audio chain starts in STATUS_SYNCING (audio.c, L238): fill_audio_out_buffers, L943 refuses to declare victory until the device-side queue is actually full, at which point the status flips to STATUS_READY with the log line “audio ready” (audio.c, L946). Only then does the restart handler start the device. That is why mpv is silent for a beat on startup: it is deliberately buffering enough audio to survive a scheduling hiccup before the first sample is played, the same defensive philosophy behind the underrun recovery described below.

Why mpv skips frames instead of stuttering

The frame-dropping decision is made in two places that cooperate. Inside the core, check_framedrop, L354 runs while both audio and video are playing. It computes how many frames the decoder is behind — (mpctx->last_av_difference - 0.010) / frame_time, clamped to 0..100 — and tells the decoder wrapper to produce that many fewer frames. The code comments call it “a crappy heuristic; avoid getting upset by incorrect fps”, which is refreshingly honest: it bails out on suspicious container frame rates below 20 or above 500 rather than trying to be clever.

Downstream, the video-output thread does its own accounting at presentation time. In render_frame, L921, a frame whose end time has already passed is marked dropped_frame before it is ever drawn (vo.c, L959), the count is bumped at vo.c, L994, and wakeup_core() tells the playback loop to fetch the next frame immediately. Dropping a frame costs one missed presentation slot; stuttering costs an audible underrun and a visible freeze. The core even measures the audio side for trouble: fill_audio_out_buffers, L969 logs “Audio device underrun detected” and restarts the device rather than pretending nothing happened. Fine-grained A/V correction is separate again — adjust_sync, L382 nudges the internal delay toward the audio timeline by a bounded amount per frame, so small clock drift is absorbed invisibly while large gaps trigger the drop path instead.

The demuxer: a thread that is always ahead

The demuxer is the reason the rest of the player can be simple. demux_start_thread, L1237 spawns demux_thread, L2746, whose loop is three lines: do one unit of thread_work, L2707 — read a packet via read_packet, L2323, execute a queued seek, switch tracks, or update caches — and if there was nothing to do, sleep until the next cache maintenance deadline. The reader-side state, struct demux_internal at demux.c, L165, owns the packet queues and the locking; the core only ever pulls from them through the non-blocking async API and inspects snapshots through demux_get_reader_state, L4873 (the same snapshot the EOF handler at handle_eof, L1279 consults before ending a file).

Memory does not grow without bound: prune_old_packets, L2464 discards packets behind the reader unless you explicitly asked for caching, and update_cache, L4527 maintains the seekable byte ranges that make a backward seek instant. This is the same division of labor you can see in FFmpeg’s own I/O layer and in VLC’s input manager — but mpv keeps it in one 5000-line file instead of a framework.

Worth noting is what all of this is not: it is not a busy poller. When thread_work, L2755 reports nothing to do, the demuxer thread sleeps on a condition variable until the next cache-maintenance deadline (demux.c, L2758). The core applies the same trick in reverse — several handlers set bounded timeouts like 0.1 or 0.2 seconds via mp_set_timeout, L74 (L691, L785) — but a timeout is always the fallback, never the signal path. Producers call wakeups: packets arriving, a frame finishing presentation, a vsync interrupt, all of them end in wakeup_core() rather than in waiting out a timer. That is how one core thread can serve audio, video, subtitles, OSD and input without ever burning a CPU core while a movie plays.

From player/core.c to player/main.c

Every source tour runs into drift, and this one ran into a notable piece: the legendary player/core.c no longer exists on master. The entry point and lifecycle functions (mpv_main, mp_create, mp_initialize) live in player/main.c, the central MPContext struct lives in player/core.h, and the file-loading logic moved into loadfile.c. Anyone following old blog posts or stack-overflow answers that cite core.c will be chasing a ghost — the line numbers in this post were all verified against the current tree.

Build facts observed during the tour, straight from the tree:

  • The project targets version 0.42.0-UNKNOWN per the root MPV_VERSION file — the -UNKNOWN suffix signals a non-release checkout, exactly what you get cloning master.
  • The build is meson-only: the root meson.build, L1 declares the project with meson_version: '>=1.3.0' at L6, and there is no configure script or alternative build system anywhere in the tree.
  • FFmpeg is the load-bearing dependency with pinned floors: libavcodec >= 60.31.102 (L23), libavformat >= 60.16.100 (L25), libavutil >= 58.29.100 (L26), libswresample >= 4.12.100 (L27), plus libass >= 0.12.2 for subtitle rendering at L33.
  • Subproject fallbacks are enabled for ffmpeg and libass (L49-L51), so a fresh clone can build its own copies instead of hunting system packages — a pattern worth copying if you maintain C projects that depend on fast-moving libraries.

If you want to see how other projects in this space structure the same problem, the FFmpeg tour covers the decoding libraries underneath mpv, the VLC tour covers a much larger player framework, and the Alacritty tour is a good contrast in terminal-side vsync handling.

Honest Limits

  • Everything here reflects commit fe753a782461 (master, November 2026). mpv moves fast; run_playloop’s handler list and the demuxer internals have been reshuffled repeatedly in the past, so re-verify line numbers before citing them in a patch or bug report.
  • The frame-drop heuristic in check_framedrop only applies to ordinary playback with audio as the clock: the source gates it on opts->frame_dropping & 2, both chains playing, and sane container fps, so --audio-only files, untimed audio outputs, and display-sync modes follow different timing paths not covered in this post.
  • The exact behavior of pause/resume depends on your audio driver: ao_set_paused() is defined in audio/out/buffer.c, and pull-style or untimed AOs handle the paused state differently from push-style ones; the underrun-recovery code even carries a comment “(Buggy if AO underruns.)” for the gapless case.
  • This tour is deliberately single-file deep. The Lua/JavaScript client API, the --vo=gpu-next render abstraction, and hardware decoding each have their own subdirectories and were not covered here.
entry.summary: A source tour of the mpv player core: run_playloop, the demuxer thread, the video chain, frame dropping, and what happens between pressing space and hearing audio.

entry.title: OBS Studio source tour: where a dropped frame actually dies in libobs

link.title: OBS Studio source tour: where a dropped frame actually dies in libobs

entry.content:
Your stream sits at 20 fps. The OBS stats window says “skipped frames due to rendering lag,” your GPU is nowhere near 100%, and none of your sources report errors. You are not alone in finding this maddening, because the answer is not in the settings dialog at all — it is one specific line inside libobs, the C core underneath the OBS Studio frontend, where a frame that missed its deadline gets quietly converted into a counter increment and forgotten. Once you have seen that line, “rendering lag” stops being a mystery and becomes a measurement problem.

libobs is not a media player and not a compositor in the browser sense. It is a small, strict real-time scheduler: exactly one graphics thread wakes up at your configured frame interval — 33.3 ms at 30 fps, 16.6 ms at 60 — walks a composable graph of sources and scenes, renders the whole stack into one texture, stages it for encoders, and then tries to sleep precisely until the next deadline. Audio runs on a completely separate thread that never touches the GPU, mixing 1024-frame chunks of PCM on its own wall-clock rhythm. The two paths only meet at the output, right before encoding.

This tour walks the master branch of obsproject/obs-studio the way a frame would travel: from int main in the Qt frontend, through the single graphics thread loop, down the scene render chain to individual draw calls, and out toward encoders and outputs. Every symbol below was verified against the actual tree — including one rename that trips up older documentation. If you enjoy this kind of tour, we have done the same for FFmpeg, SDL, and Godot on this site; links are sprinkled where they help.

The libobs core at a glance: one Qt frontend, one 60 Hz graphics thread, one independent audio mixer thread, and outputs that consume both streams.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • The process starts in ordinary Qt territory: main, L887 parses command-line arguments, installs crash handling, and constructs the OBSApp Qt object before any OBS-specific machinery exists.
  • The frontend then boots the core with obs_startup, L1330, which is deliberately one-shot — call it twice and it logs a warning and refuses.
  • Video bring-up happens in obs_init_video, L695, which builds the canvas and video mixes, and then spawns the graphics thread, L720 with a plain pthread_create.
  • That thread’s body is obs_graphics_thread, L1161, a while loop over obs_graphics_thread_loop, L1097 — the heartbeat of the whole program.
  • Each iteration first ticks every source via tick_sources, L32, which calls obs_source_video_tick, L82 on each source in the main list.
  • Rendering is orchestrated by output_frame, L871, which calls render_video, L541 and then downloads or hands off the finished texture.
  • The actual pixel work bottoms out in scene_video_render, L1059, which walks the scene’s linked list of items and draws each visible one.
  • After rendering, video_sleep, L808 targets the next frame deadline; a missed target is where lagged frames are born.
  • Audio never joins this loop: audio_thread, L205 sleeps to its own deadlines and emits mixed PCM in fixed chunks.

The detail view: the init sequence on the left, the graphics-thread loop in the middle (tick chain, render chain, sleep and FPS accounting), the audio thread at the bottom, and the output capture path on the right.

The heartbeat: one graphics thread, one loop

The most important architectural decision in libobs is that there is exactly one thread that renders. obs_graphics_thread, L1161 sets a thread name (“libobs: graphics thread”), computes the frame interval once, and then loops. Inside obs_graphics_thread_loop, L1097 the per-frame order is fixed: update active states, tick sources at tick_sources, L1112, pump the render pass through output_frames, L1125, paint preview windows with render_displays, L94, execute queued graphics tasks, and only then sleep.

One consequence: everything shares one frame budget. A heavy source filter, a slow capture device, and even an expensive preview paint all draw from the same 16.6 ms allowance. This is a different shape from SDL, where you own the loop yourself, and from Godot, where the engine separates process and render phases — see our Godot scene-tree tour. libobs gives you neither: the loop is fixed, and your sources are guests inside it.

Where a 20 fps stream actually dies

Here is the line you came for. video_sleep, L808 computes the next deadline as cur_time + interval_ns and calls os_sleepto_ns, L815. If the sleep succeeds, one frame was produced on schedule. If it fails — meaning the tick-plus-render work already overran the interval — the function counts how many whole intervals were missed, and records them: lagged_frames, L828 adds count - 1 to the mix’s running total. That counter is what surfaces later as “lagged frames” in the frontend’s statistics.

Note what this implies for your 20 fps mystery. Frames are not “dropped” by the encoder at that point; they die before encoding, in the pacing function, because the loop arrived late. The per-second bookkeeping that publishes the measured rate happens just after the sleep, in the FPS accounting block at video_fps, L1149. So the diagnostic order is: if lagged frames rise while the GPU is idle, something in the tick or render path is blocking on the CPU (a slow source callback, a lock, disk I/O in a filter); if lagged frames rise with the GPU saturated, you are simply asking for more pixels than the machine can rasterize in one interval.

Scenes are just sources: the render chain

The composable part of libobs is elegant. A scene is itself an obs_source — obs_scene_create, L1794 returns an ordinary source handle — which means scenes nest inside scenes and the renderer does not care. When the graphics thread needs pixels, render_main_texture, L172 clears the render target, runs any registered draw callbacks, and then calls obs_view_render, L202. The view walks its fixed set of channels — obs_view_render, L118 iterates MAX_CHANNELS slots — and calls obs_source_video_render, L135 on whatever source is bound to each.

For a scene source, that dispatch lands in scene_video_render, L1059, which takes the video lock, then walks the first_item linked list at scene items loop, L1077 and calls render_item on each visible entry. Every draw goes through the effect system: an effect is a shader bundle whose parameters are looked up with gs_effect_get_param_by_name, L275 and uploaded with setters like gs_effect_set_float, L436. After the main texture exists, render_convert_texture, L566 converts RGBA to planar YUV on the GPU — a step our FFmpeg tour revisits from the other side, where encoders consume exactly that planar layout.

The tick side mirrors the render side. obs_source_video_tick, L1406 handles async video buffers, audio action queues, and filter timing for every source, and a scene’s own scene_video_tick, L990 advances item transforms and visibility transitions. Tick and render are deliberately decoupled: state mutates during the tick, then is read to paint during the render pass.

Audio never touches the graphics thread

Audio is the second half of the story and runs on its own clock. During startup, obs_init_audio, L907 configures sample rate and speaker layout and opens the audio subsystem through audio_output_open, L353, which spawns its thread at pthread_create, L376. That thread is audio_thread, L205: an infinite loop that computes a wall-clock deadline 1024 samples ahead — the chunk size is the compile-time constant AUDIO_OUTPUT_FRAMES, L31 — sleeps to it with a fast path at os_sleepto_ns_fast, L227, and then runs input_and_output, L160.

The mixing itself is refreshingly boring: sum every registered input’s float planes into a mix buffer, clamp, convert to the output format, and invoke the registered callback — once per mix, per chunk. Because deadlines are wall-clock anchored rather than “1024 samples after the last work finished,” a slow mixing pass does not accumulate drift; it either makes the deadline or the buffer underruns audibly. On Windows the thread even registers itself with MMCSS via AvSetMmThreadCharacteristics so the scheduler treats it gently. This is the same separation of clocks we saw in the FFmpeg scheduling model: video paced by frame intervals, audio paced by sample counts, reconciled only at the mux — start there.

From CMake presets to pixels

Building OBS from source tells you a lot about how the core is organized. The root CMakeLists.txt, L1 demands CMake 3.28–3.30 — a notably modern floor — and pulls in a bootstrap script from cmake/common/ before the project is even declared. The component layout is explicit: ENABLE_FRONTEND, L18 gates the Qt UI (it requires Qt and can be switched off to build headless libobs consumers), and the renderer backends are separate plugins: libobs-d3d11, L24 plus libobs-winrt on Windows, libobs-opengl, L27 elsewhere, libobs-metal, L29 on macOS. The frontend is added last, at add_subdirectory(frontend), L35.

One fact worth flagging for anyone following old tutorials: the Qt code no longer lives in a top-level UI/ directory. It moved to frontend/, the class is OBSApp (constructor at OBSApp::OBSApp, L959), and the entry point moved with it into frontend/obs-main.cpp. For this tour we cloned the repository sparsely (only libobs, frontend, and cmake), which yielded roughly 5,700 tracked paths total and made grepping the C core comfortable on a laptop.

Honest Limits

  • Line numbers refer to the master branch as cloned on 2026-11-13 (commit fe1ed7955f30). The GitHub blob/master/ links above will drift as files are edited; symbols are stable, lines are not.
  • Older documentation and some third-party diagrams mention a function named obs_video_tick. It no longer exists in master; the loop is obs_graphics_thread_loop. We re-derived the tick path from the tree rather than trusting prior art.
  • The diagrams trace the core frame path only. Encoder internals (x264, NVENC, the encoder-group logic visible around video_sleep), plugin sources like display/window capture, and the scripting layer live outside the traced files and are not covered.
  • The audio section describes the audio-io thread’s pacing and mixing; the deeper per-source audio path (timestamp offsets and buffering on the way into the mixer) is a separate libobs file we did not verify line-by-line for this tour.
  • “Rendering lag” has other contributors we deliberately excluded: GPU driver behavior, VSync interactions of the preview, and Windows-specific timer resolution are real but not observable from this repository alone.
entry.summary: A guided walk through OBS Studio's libobs core in C: the 60 Hz graphics thread, the scene render chain, the separate audio mixer thread, and the exact line where lagged frames are counted.
